title: 9 Laws Every Manager Should Know (And Most Break Daily)
author: The Good Boss
summary: The Good Boss newsletter lays out nine informal 'laws' of management, arguing they function like laws of physics or economics that govern team behavior but are almost never taught explicitly. Each law is illustrated with a concrete manager story: an engineering manager whose 'story points per sprint' metric backfired under Goodhart's Law once the team learned to game it, a platform-team manager who discovered via Parkinson's Law that a 'three-week' migration could actually be done in four days once real pressure forced it, and a cross-functional manager who saw one junior engineer's public pushback unlock a culture shift under the Bannister Effect. The piece treats these patterns as predictable and manageable rather than surprising, urging leaders to design around them. It is written as a numbered listicle-style deep dive.
points: Frames nine unwritten 'laws' of management as physics-like patterns leaders discover through experience rather than training.
Uses concrete manager vignettes (Elena, Marcus, Simone) to make each abstract law tangible and memorable.
Goodhart's Law example shows how a proxy metric (story points) gets gamed the moment it becomes the target.
Parkinson's Law example reveals that a 'three-week' estimate compressed into four days once genuine urgency hit, exposing padded timelines.
The Bannister Effect example shows how publicly rewarding one person's dissent can shift an entire team's willingness to speak up.
quotes: Every industry has its unwritten rules. Just like physics has laws, and economics has laws, so does leadership.
The only difference is that nobody bothers to write them down in a management training.
When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
That's Goodhart's Law in action: the moment you tell people what you're measuring, you've told them exactly where to cut corners.
Marcus told me that was the moment he stopped trusting his own estimates.
Once one person proves a limit was never real, everyone behind them moves faster.
It wasn't a rule or culture code written anywhere. It was just how the team had always worked.
